source_text: Ἐδόκει τῇ μόνῃ ἐκ τῶν γονέων κήδεσθαι ἡμῶν περιλειπομένῃ μητρὶ τ᾽ ἄλλα ἐκπαιδευομένους, οἷα παῖδας οὐκ ἀγεννεῖς δῆθεν καὶ φύντας καὶ τρεφομένους, φοιτᾶν καὶ ῥήτορι, ὡς δὴ ῥήτορας ἐσομένους. καὶ δῆτα ἐφοιτῶμεν, καὶ ῥήτορας μὲν οὐκ εἰς μακρὰν ἔσεσθαι ἡμᾶς ἔλεγον, οἱ τότε κρίνοντες οὕτως. οὐκ ἔγωγε τοῦτο λέγειν οὔτε οἶδα, οὔτ᾽ ἂν θελήσαιμι· λόγος δὲ οὐδεὶς ἦν τούτων, οὐδέ τις καταβολή· οὐδέπω τῶν τῇδε φέρειν ἡμᾶς δυναμένων αἰτιῶν. ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἄγρυπνος ὢν ὁ θεῖος παιδαγωγὸς, καὶ ἀληθὴς κηδεμὼν, οὔτε τῶν οἰκείων διανοουμένων, οὔτε καὶ ἐμοῦ αὐτοῦ προθυμουμένου, ἐπῆν, συμβαλών τινι τῶν ἐμῶν διδασκάλων, ἄλλως τὴν Ῥωμαίων φωνὴν ἐκπαιδεύειν με πεπιστευμένῳ· οὐχ ὡς ἐπ᾽ ἄκρον ἥξοντα, ὡς δὲ μὴ ἄπειρος εἴην πάντῃ καὶ τῆσδε τῆς φωνῆς, ἔτυχε δὲ νόμων οὐκ ἄπειρος ὤν. τοῦτο ἐπὶ νοῦν βαλὼν, προὐτρέψατό με δι᾽ αὐτοῦ τῶν Ῥωμαίων ἐκμανθάνειν νόμους. καὶ λιπαρῶς γε τοῦτο ἐποίει ὁ ἀνὴρ ἐκεῖνος, κἀγὼ μέν τι ἐπειθόμην, τἀνδρὶ μᾶλλον χαριζόμενος, ἤπερ τῆς τέχνης ἐραστὴς ὤν. ὁ δέ με λαβὼν ἀκροατὴν, φιλοτίμως μὲν διδάσκειν ἤρχετο. ἐπεφθέγξατο δέ τι, ὅ μοι ἀληθέστατα πάντων ἀποβέβηκε· μέγιστον ἔσεσθαί μοι ἐφόδιον. (τοῦτο γὰρ τοὔνομα ἐκεῖνος ὠνόμασεν.) εἴτε τις ῥήτωρ τῶν ἐν τοῖς δικαστηρίοις ἀγωνιζομένων, εἴτε καὶ ἄλλος τις εἶναι θελήσαιμι, τὴν μάθησιν τῶν νόμων. ὁ μὲν οὕτως ἀπεφθέγξατο, τείνων εἰς τὰ ἀνθρώπινα τὸν λόγον. ἐμοὶ δὲ ἀτεχνῶς ὑπό τινι θειοτέρᾳ ἐπιπνοίᾳ ἀποφοιβάσαι δοκεῖ τῆς αὐτοῦ ὑπολήψεως. ἐπεὶ γὰρ ἐξεπαιδευόμην ἑκὼν καὶ ἄκων τοὺς νόμους τούσδε, δεσμοὶ μέν πως ἤδη κατεβέβληντο καὶ αἰτία καὶ ἀφορμὴ τῆς ἐπὶ τάδε ὁδοῦ, ἡ τῶν Βηρυτίων πόλις. ἡ δὲ, οὐ μακρὰν ἀπέχουσα τῶν ἐνταῦθα πόλις Ῥωμαϊκωτέρα πως, καὶ τῶν νόμων τούτων εἶναι πιστευθεῖσα παιδευτήριον. τὸν δὲ ἱερὸν τοῦτον ἄνδρα ἐκ τῆς Αἰγύπτου ἐκ τῆς Ἀλεξανδρέων πόλεως, ἔνθα τὴν ἑστίαν ἔχων, ἔτυχε πρότερον, καὶ αὐτὸν ἐκίνει καὶ μετῴκιζεν ἐπὶ τόδε τὸ χωρίον ὥσπερ ἀπαντήσοντα ἡμῖν, ἕτερα πράγματα. οὐκ ἔγωγε καὶ ταῦτα αἰτιολογεῖσθαι ὅτι οἶδα, καὶ ἑκὼν παρήσω. οὐ μὴν ἀλλ᾽ οὔπω γε τῆς ἐνθάδε μοι ἀφίξεως καὶ τῆς πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα συμπλοκῆς, οὐδὲν οὕτως ἀναγκαῖον ἦν, ὅσον ἐπὶ τοῖς νόμοις ἡμῶν, δυνατὸν ὂν καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν Ῥωμαίων ἀποδημῆσαι πόλιν.
thought_title: Rhetoric, Latin, and the study of Roman law
orientation: His mother sends him to study rhetoric, and a teacher of Latin points him toward Roman law.
pass_a_gloss: It seemed good to the mother, the only one of the parents left remaining to care for (kedesthai) us, that we, being educated (ekpaideuomenous) in the other things, as boys not ill-born (agenneis), forsooth (dethen), both in birth and in rearing, should attend (phoitan) a rhetor (rhetor) also, as going to be rhetors. And indeed we attended, and those then judging so said we would before long be rhetors. I neither know how to say this, nor would I wish to; but there was no account (logos) of these things, nor any foundation (katabole), the causes able to bring us here not yet being [present]. But being wakeful (agrypnos), the divine tutor (paidagogos) and true guardian (kedemon), while neither my household were considering it nor I myself eager for it, came upon [it] (epen), meeting with (symbalon) one of my teachers, who had been entrusted otherwise merely with teaching me the voice (phone) of the Romans, not as going to reach the top, but that I might not be wholly inexperienced in this voice also; and he happened to be not inexperienced in laws (nomoi). Having put this to mind, he urged (proutrepsato) me through him to learn thoroughly the laws of the Romans. And that man did this persistently (liparos), and I obeyed somewhat, gratifying (charizomenos) the man rather than being a lover (erastes) of the art (techne). He, taking me as hearer (akroates), began to teach ambitiously (philotimos). And he uttered something which has turned out most truly of all for me: that the learning (mathesis) of the laws would be my greatest provision for the journey (ephodion) (for this name he named), whether I should wish to be some rhetor of those contending in the courts (dikasteria), or anything else. He thus spoke, stretching his word toward human things. But to me he seems simply, under some more divine inspiration (epipnoia), to have prophesied (apophoibasai) beyond his own supposition (hypolepsis). For when I was being educated, willing and unwilling, in these laws, bonds (desmoi) had somehow already been laid down, and cause (aitia) and starting point (aphorme) of the road (hodos) to here: the city of the Berytians. And it, a city not far distant from here, somewhat more Roman, and trusted to be a school (paideuterion) of these laws. And this sacred (hieros) man, from Egypt, from the city of the Alexandrians, where he formerly happened to have his hearth (hestia), other affairs (pragmata) moved and transferred to this place, as if going to meet us. I do not know how to give the causes of these things also, and willingly will pass them by. Nevertheless, there was not yet anything so necessary (anankaion) for my arrival here and my joining (symploke) with the man, so far as concerns our laws, it being possible also to go abroad to the city of the Romans.

pass_b_english: My mother, the only one of my parents left to care for us, decided that, since we were being educated in the other subjects as boys of good birth and upbringing, as of course we were, we should also attend a teacher of rhetoric, in the expectation that we would become orators. So we attended him, and those who judged such things at the time said that we would soon be orators. For my part, I could not say this, nor would I want to. But there was as yet no thought of all this, nor any groundwork laid for it, for none of the causes that could carry us here was yet at work.

But the divine tutor, ever wakeful, the true guardian, stepped in when neither my family had thought of it nor I myself desired it, and fell in with one of my teachers. This teacher had been entrusted simply with teaching me the Roman tongue, not so that I would master it, but so that I might not be wholly ignorant of this language too; and he happened also to be no stranger to the law. Taking note of this, my guardian urged me through him to learn the laws of the Romans. That man pressed this on me earnestly, and I went along with him to some degree, more to please him than because I loved the art. Taking me as his student, he set about teaching me with zeal. And he said something that has come true for me more truly than anything: that the study of the laws would be my greatest provision for the journey (that was the very word he used), whether I wished to be one of the orators who contend in the law courts, or anything else. He said this with his eye on human affairs. But it seems to me that, under some more divine inspiration, he prophesied beyond what he himself supposed.

For while I was being trained in these laws, willingly and unwillingly, bonds of a sort were already laid down, and the cause and occasion of my road here: the city of Berytus. That city, not far from here, is somewhat more Roman in character and is trusted as the school of these laws. As for this holy man, other affairs moved him from Egypt, from the city of Alexandria, where he had happened to make his home before, and brought him to this place, as if to meet us. I do not know how to give the causes of these things either, and I will gladly pass them by. Even so, nothing yet made my coming here and my meeting with the man necessary, as far as our law studies went, since it was also possible to travel to the city of Rome.
notes: 'As of course we were' renders the ironic particle dethen. 'There was as yet no thought of all this': logos oudeis en touton; 'all this' refers to the things that brought Gregory to Caesarea. The divine tutor (paidagogos) and true guardian (kedemon) is the guardian angel of 4.2 (compare 5.3, 'the divine angel'), so these titles stay lowercase. 'Fell in with' renders symbalon tini (meeting, engaging with); the teacher was already Gregory's Latin teacher. 'Taking note of this, my guardian urged me through him': the subject of proutrepsato is the divine tutor and di' autou ('through him') is the teacher, so the tutor works through the teacher (the Latin 'ipso docente' says the same in other words). The print has 'kago men ti epeithomen' ('I went along ... to some degree'); Koetschau reads 'mentoi' ('and I did obey'). 'Provision for the journey' (ephodion) is Gregory's own word and anticipates the journey he goes on to tell. 'Prophesied' renders apophoibasai, to utter as an oracle. Berytus is modern Beirut. The last sentence follows the Greek; the Latin column reads it a little differently ('by which I could have gone to Rome through our laws'). No Scripture quoted or alluded to.
